findings.evidence:
## Restraint and self-critique

Spend your boldness in one place. Let the signature element be the one memorable thing, keep everything around it quiet and disciplined, and cut any decoration that does not serve the brief. Not taking a risk can be a risk itself! Build to a quality floor without announcing it: responsive down to mobile, visible keyboard focus, reduced motion respected. Critique your own work as you build, taking screenshots if your environment supports it – a picture is worth 1000 tokens. Consider Chanel's advice: before leaving the house, take a look in the mirror and remove one accessory. Human creators have memory and always try to do something new, so if you have a space to quickly jot down notes about what you've tried, it can help you in future passes. After building, read through the final CSS top to bottom and hand-count every pair of selectors whose specificity conflicts, listing each pair.
findings.why: The Restraint and self-critique section interleaves at least five sequential actions in one prose block — build to the quality floor, critique during the build, take screenshots, jot iteration notes, then audit the final CSS — so steps get lost and skipped.
findings.fix: Break the section into an ordered list: 1) quality floor checklist, 2) in-build critique with screenshots, 3) iteration notes, 4) post-build CSS audit.

findings.evidence: If the brief does not pin down what the product or subject is, pin it yourself before designing: name one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job, and state your choice. If there's any information in your memory about the human's preferences, context about what they're building, or designs you've made before – use that as a hint. The subject's own world, its materials, instruments, artifacts, and vernacular, is where distinctive choices come from. Build with the brief's real content and subject matter throughout. Never ask the user clarifying questions about the brief; make every decision yourself and present the finished result.
findings.why: The skill affirmatively forbids ever asking the human, and line 39 additionally tells the agent to withhold ideas until confident — there is no escalation point anywhere, so a wrong guess about the product or audience burns the entire deliverable silently.
findings.fix: Permit one narrow escalation: when the subject/audience guess is low-confidence, state the assumption to the user before the build pass (or ask one clarifying question); keep the no-questions default for everything else.

findings.evidence:
Work in two passes. First, brainstorm a short design plan based on the human's design brief: create a compact token system covering color, type, layout, and a signature element. Record your token system in references/tokens.md before building. Save wireframe sketches under assets\wireframes\ as you go.

Then write the code, deriving every color and type decision from your plan.

Try to do a lot of this planning and iteration in your thinking, and only show ideas to the user when you have higher confidence it'll delight them.

findings.fix: Add a do-not-skip guard: "Do not start writing page code until the token system is written down, even when the design feels obvious" — and drop the sentence encouraging planning to stay in thinking.

##### Frontmatter

Write the YAML frontmatter with `name` and `description`:

- `name`: The skill name
- `description`: This is the primary triggering mechanism for your skill, and helps Claude understand when to use the skill.
  - Include both what the Skill does and specific triggers/contexts for when to use it.
  - Include all "when to use" information here - Not in the body. The body is only loaded after triggering, so "When to Use This Skill" sections in the body are not helpful to Claude.

Do not include any other fields in YAML frontmatter.

For reference, the full set of frontmatter validation rules:

| Field | Rule | Limit | On violation |
|---|---|---|---|
| name | required, non-empty | 64 chars | validation error |
| name | letters, digits, hyphens only | - | validation error |
| name | matches the skill directory name | - | validation error |
| description | required, non-empty | 1024 chars | validation error |

| license | optional, free text | 128 chars | warning |
| compatibility | optional | 500 chars | warning |

Write the YAML frontmatter with `name` and `description`:

- `name`: The skill name
- `description`: This is the primary triggering mechanism for your skill, and helps Claude understand when to use the skill.
  - Include both what the Skill does and specific triggers/contexts for when to use it.
  - Include all "when to use" information here - Not in the body. The body is only loaded after triggering, so "When to Use This Skill" sections in the body are not helpful to Claude.

Do not include any other fields in YAML frontmatter.

For reference, the full set of frontmatter validation rules:

| Field | Rule | Limit | On violation |
|---|---|---|---|
| name | required, non-empty | 64 chars | validation error |
| name | letters, digits, hyphens only | - | validation error |
| name | matches the skill directory name | - | validation error |
| description | required, non-empty | 1024 chars | validation error |
| description | no XML or HTML tags | - | validation error |
| description | third person, states when to use | - | warning |
| license | optional, free text | 128 chars | warning |
| compatibility | optional | 500 chars | warning |
| metadata | optional key-value map | 10 keys | extra keys dropped |
| metadata keys | lowercase, hyphenated | 64 chars | key renamed |
| frontmatter block | valid YAML, closed with --- | 100 lines | validation error |
findings.why: This blanket ban contradicts the anatomy section ("plus optional fields like license, metadata, and compatibility") and the table four lines below that validates license, compatibility, and metadata as allowed — the agent writing frontmatter cannot tell which rule to follow.
findings.fix: Keep one rule: either allow the documented optional fields and delete the ban, or ban them everywhere and remove the optional rows from the table and the anatomy section.

findings.evidence:
### Step 1: Understanding the Skill with Concrete Examples

Skip this step only when the skill's usage patterns are already clearly understood. It remains valuable even when working with an existing skill.

To create an effective skill, clearly understand concrete examples of how the skill will be used. This understanding can come from either direct user examples or generated examples that are validated with user feedback.
findings.why: The skip condition is self-certified — an agent can always reason that patterns are "clearly understood" — so nothing actually guards the interview step that the whole process depends on.
findings.fix: Gate skipping on concrete evidence, e.g. skip only when the user has already supplied example requests or explicit functionality requirements.

### Step 5: Iterate

After testing the skill, users may request improvements. Often this happens right after using the skill, with fresh context of how the skill performed.

**Iteration workflow:**

1. Use the skill on real tasks
2. Notice struggles or inefficiencies
3. Identify how SKILL.md or bundled resources should be updated
4. Implement changes and test again

findings.fix: Reference scripts/package_skill.py in the workflow (e.g. a package-for-distribution step after validation), or state explicitly that packaging is out of scope.

# Output Patterns

Use these patterns when skills need to produce consistent, high-quality output.

## Examples Pattern

For skills where output quality depends on seeing examples, provide input/output pairs:

```markdown
## Commit message format

Generate commit messages following these examples:

**Example 1:**
Input: Added user authentication with JWT tokens
Output:
```
feat(auth): implement JWT-based authentication

Add login endpoint and token validation middleware
```

**Example 2:**
Input: Fixed bug where dates displayed incorrectly in reports
Output:
```
fix(reports): correct date formatting in timezone conversion

Use UTC timestamps consistently across report generation
```

Follow this style: type(scope): brief description, then detailed explanation.
```

Examples help Claude understand the desired style and level of detail more clearly than descriptions alone.
findings.why: SKILL.md sends readers here "for template and example patterns", but the file contains only the examples pattern. An author whose skill must emit a strict output format finds no template/skeleton pattern — the promised guidance is absent.
findings.fix: Add a Template Pattern section (a skeleton with placeholders plus guidance on when to demand strict adherence vs. treat it as a starting point), or correct the SKILL.md pointer to promise only example patterns.

findings.evidence:
##### Frontmatter

Write the YAML frontmatter with `name` and `description`:

- `name`: The skill name
- `description`: This is the primary triggering mechanism for your skill, and helps Claude understand when to use the skill.
  - Include both what the Skill does and specific triggers/contexts for when to use it.
  - Include all "when to use" information here - Not in the body. The body is only loaded after triggering, so "When to Use This Skill" sections in the body are not helpful to Claude.

Do not include any other fields in YAML frontmatter.
findings.why: The file states the rules for descriptions (what plus when, third person) and calls the description the primary triggering mechanism, but gives no example of an effective description anywhere in the skill or its references. At the single highest-stakes spot in skill authoring, a concrete example would change what authors write.
findings.fix: Add one worked example of a good description (what + when + trigger contexts) next to the rules, optionally paired with a bad what-only counterexample.

findings.evidence:
At this point, it is time to actually create the skill.

Skip this step only if the skill being developed already exists, and iteration is needed. In this case, continue to the next step.

When creating a new skill from scratch, always run the `init_skill.py` script. The script conveniently generates a new template skill directory that automatically includes everything a skill requires, making the skill creation process much more efficient and reliable. The script tracks the latest revision of the skill format, and skills initialized with it are accepted by all current Claude releases.
findings.why: "Tracks the latest revision of the skill format" and "accepted by all current Claude releases" are undated claims that silently go stale the moment the format or a release changes, with no date or version to signal staleness.
findings.fix: Drop the compatibility claim, or state the format revision the script targets and the date it was last verified.

findings.evidence:
## Skill Creation Process

Skill creation involves these steps:

1. Understand the skill with concrete examples
2. Plan reusable skill contents (scripts, references, assets)
3. Initialize the skill (run init_skill.py)
4. Edit the skill (implement resources and write SKILL.md)
5. Iterate based on real usage
findings.why: The process runs understand, plan, init, edit, iterate — no step validates the created skill, even though scripts/quick_validate.py and scripts/package_skill.py are bundled and never mentioned in the body. The output is treated as one-shot: a skill with invalid frontmatter (like a missing name) ships undetected, so "creating effective skills" fails at exactly the mechanical errors the bundled validator catches.
findings.fix: Add a validation step between editing and iterating: run scripts/quick_validate.py on the skill directory, fix failures and re-run until it passes; mention scripts/package_skill.py for producing a distributable .skill file.

findings.evidence:
### Build Rationalization Table

Capture rationalizations from baseline testing (see Testing section below). Every excuse agents make goes in the table:

```markdown
| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Too simple to test" | Simple code breaks. Test takes 30 seconds. |
| "I'll test after" | Tests passing immediately prove nothing. |
| "Tests after achieve same goals" | Tests-after = "what does this do?" Tests-first = "what should this do?" |
```

### Create Red Flags List

Make it easy for agents to self-check when rationalizing:

```markdown
## Red Flags - STOP and Start Over

- Code before test
- "I already manually tested it"
- "Tests after achieve the same purpose"
- "It's about spirit not ritual"
- "This is different because..."

**All of these mean: Delete code. Start over with TDD.**
```

### Update SDO for Violation Symptoms

Add to description: symptoms of when you're ABOUT to violate the rule:

```yaml
description: use when implementing any feature or bugfix, before writing implementation code
```

findings.evidence:
## Bulletproofing Skills Against Rationalization

Skills that enforce discipline (like TDD) need to resist rationalization. Agents are smart and will find loopholes when under pressure.

**Scope:** this toolkit is for discipline failures — an agent that knows the rule and skips it under pressure. For wrong-shaped output or omitted elements, prohibition-based bulletproofing backfires; use the forms in Match the Form to the Failure instead.

**Psychology note:** Understanding WHY persuasion techniques work helps you apply them systematically. See persuasion-principles.md for research foundation (Cialdini, 2021; Meincke et al., 2025) on authority, commitment, scarcity, social proof, and unity principles.

### Close Every Loophole Explicitly

Don't just state the rule - forbid specific workarounds:

<Bad>
```markdown
Write code before test? Delete it.
```
</Bad>

<Good>
```markdown
Write code before test? Delete it. Start over.

**No exceptions:**
- Don't keep it as "reference"
- Don't "adapt" it while writing tests
- Don't look at it
- Delete means delete
```
</Good>
findings.why: This bulletproofing toolkit, including the worked before/after example, is duplicated near-verbatim in testing-skills-with-subagents.md ("Plugging Each Hole"), and the RED/GREEN/REFACTOR mapping table is also duplicated across both files. The body totals 3,788 words against the skill's own "<500 words" target for non-frequently-loaded skills (lines 217-221) — once-per-creation reference material that meets the skill's own definition of detail that belongs in a separate file.
findings.fix: Keep the bulletproofing/plugging-holes toolkit in one file and link to it from the other; drop the duplicated TDD mapping table from one of the two files.

findings.evidence:
### REFACTOR: Close Loopholes

Agent found new rationalization? Add explicit counter. Re-test until bulletproof.
findings.why: The description promises "verifying skills work before deployment", but when the REFACTOR loop fails to converge — the agent keeps finding new rationalizations — the only instruction is to re-test again, with no point where the agent stops and asks the human. The mandatory deployment checklist then ends in a git commit and push with no human confirmation gate.
findings.fix: Add an escalation rule (e.g. after a set number of failed REFACTOR cycles, stop and report to the human) and a confirm-before-push step in the deployment checklist.

findings.evidence:
## Match the Form to the Failure

Before writing guidance, classify the baseline failure. The form that bulletproofs one failure type measurably backfires on another.

| Baseline failure | Right form | Wrong form |
|---|---|---|
| Skips/violates a rule under pressure (knows better, does it anyway) | Prohibition + rationalization table + red flags (see Bulletproofing below) | Soft guidance ("prefer...", "consider...") |
| Complies, but output has the wrong shape (bloated prompt, buried verdict, restated spec) | Positive recipe or contract: state what the output IS — its parts, in order | Prohibition list ("don't restate", "never narrate") |
| Omits a required element from something they already produce | Structural: REQUIRED field or slot in the template they fill in | Prose reminders near the template |
| Behavior should depend on a condition | Conditional keyed to an observable predicate ("if the brief exists, reference it") | Unconditional rule + exemption clauses |

**Why prohibitions backfire on shaping problems:** under a competing incentive ("make the prompt self-contained"), agents negotiate with "don't X". In head-to-head wording tests on dispatch-prompt guidance, the prohibition arm produced clearly more of the unwanted content than the recipe arm (fully separated distributions), and trended worse than even the no-guidance control — micro-test your own case rather than assuming, but never reach for the prohibition by default. A recipe leaves nothing to negotiate: the output matches the stated shape or it doesn't.

**Rules for whichever form you pick:**
- **No nuance clauses.** "Don't X unless it matters" reopens the negotiation — appending a single nuance clause to a winning recipe degraded it from consistent to noisy in the same wording tests. Express a real exception as its own conditional on an observable predicate.
- **Exemption clauses don't scope.** "This limit doesn't apply to code blocks" still suppresses code blocks. If part of the output must be exempt, restructure so the rule can't reach it.

findings.fix: Add one real before/after pair — the prohibition wording and the winning recipe wording — for the dispatch-prompt case the section cites.

### Step 1: Spawn all runs (with-skill AND baseline) in the same turn

For each test case, spawn two subagents in the same turn — one with the skill, one without. This is important: don't spawn the with-skill runs first and then come back for baselines later. Launch everything at once so it all finishes around the same time.

**With-skill run:**

```
Execute this task:
- Skill path: <path-to-skill>
- Task: <eval prompt>
- Input files: <eval files if any, or "none">
- Save outputs to: <workspace>/iteration-<N>/eval-<ID>/with_skill/outputs/
- Outputs to save: <what the user cares about — e.g., "the .docx file", "the final CSV">
```

**Baseline run** (same prompt, but the baseline depends on context):
- **Creating a new skill**: no skill at all. Same prompt, no skill path, save to `without_skill/outputs/`.
- **Improving an existing skill**: the old version. Before editing, snapshot the skill (`cp -r <skill-path> <workspace>/skill-snapshot/`), then point the baseline subagent at the snapshot. Save to `old_skill/outputs/`.

Write an `eval_metadata.json` for each test case (assertions can be empty for now). Give each eval a descriptive name based on what it's testing — not just "eval-0". Use this name for the directory too. If this iteration uses new or modified eval prompts, create these files for each new eval directory — don't assume they carry over from previous iterations.

findings.fix: State a default: one run per configuration for quick iteration, 3+ runs per configuration when the user wants the variance benchmark, and say the metadata field must match what was actually run.

### Step 3: Run the optimization loop

Tell the user: "This will take some time — I'll run the optimization loop in the background and check on it periodically."

Save the eval set to the workspace, then run in the background:

```bash
python -m scripts.run_loop \
  --eval-set <path-to-trigger-eval.json> \
  --skill-path <path-to-skill> \
  --model <model-id-powering-this-session> \
  --max-iterations 5 \
  --verbose

Use the model ID from your system prompt (the one powering the current session) so the triggering test matches what the user actually experiences.

While it runs, periodically tail the output to give the user updates on which iteration it's on and what the scores look like.

This handles the full optimization loop automatically. It splits the eval set into 60% train and 40% held-out test, evaluates the current description (running each query 3 times to get a reliable trigger rate), then calls Claude to propose improvements based on what failed. It re-evaluates each new description on both train and test, iterating up to 5 times. When it's done, it opens an HTML report in the browser showing the results per iteration and returns JSON with `best_description` — selected by test score rather than train score to avoid overfitting.

findings.fix: Add "run from the skill-creator directory" next to this command, and one sentence disclosing the temporary .claude/commands/ files plus a cleanup check if the loop is interrupted.

The skill creator is liable to be used by people across a wide range of familiarity with coding jargon. findings.evidence:
## Claude.ai-specific instructions

In Claude.ai, the core workflow is the same (draft → test → review → improve → repeat), but because Claude.ai doesn't have subagents, some mechanics change. Here's what to adapt:

**Running test cases**: No subagents means no parallel execution. For each test case, read the skill's SKILL.md, then follow its instructions to accomplish the test prompt yourself. Do them one at a time. This is less rigorous than independent subagents (you wrote the skill and you're also running it, so you have full context), but it's a useful sanity check — and the human review step compensates. Skip the baseline runs — just use the skill to complete the task as requested.

**Reviewing results**: If you can't open a browser (e.g., Claude.ai's VM has no display, or you're on a remote server), skip the browser reviewer entirely. Instead, present results directly in the conversation. For each test case, show the prompt and the output. If the output is a file the user needs to see (like a .docx or .xlsx), save it to the filesystem and tell them where it is so they can download and inspect it. Ask for feedback inline: "How does this look? Anything you'd change?"

**Benchmarking**: Skip the quantitative benchmarking — it relies on baseline comparisons which aren't meaningful without subagents. Focus on qualitative feedback from the user.

**The iteration loop**: Same as before — improve the skill, rerun the test cases, ask for feedback — just without the browser reviewer in the middle. You can still organize results into iteration directories on the filesystem if you have one.

**Description optimization**: This section requires the `claude` CLI tool (specifically `claude -p`) which is only available in Claude Code. Skip it if you're on Claude.ai.

**Blind comparison**: Requires subagents. Skip it.

**Packaging**: The `package_skill.py` script works anywhere with Python and a filesystem. On Claude.ai, you can run it and the user can download the resulting `.skill` file.

**Updating an existing skill**: The user might be asking you to update an existing skill, not create a new one. In this case:
- **Preserve the original name.** Note the skill's directory name and `name` frontmatter field -- use them unchanged. E.g., if the installed skill is `research-helper`, output `research-helper.skill` (not `research-helper-v2`).
- **Copy to a writeable location before editing.** The installed skill path may be read-only. Copy to `/tmp/skill-name/`, edit there, and package from the copy.
- **If packaging manually, stage in `/tmp/` first**, then copy to the output directory -- direct writes may fail due to permissions.

---

## Cowork-Specific Instructions

If you're in Cowork, the main things to know are:

- You have subagents, so the main workflow (spawn test cases in parallel, run baselines, grade, etc.) all works. (However, if you run into severe problems with timeouts, it's OK to run the test prompts in series rather than parallel.)
- You don't have a browser or display, so when generating the eval viewer, use `--static <output_path>` to write a standalone HTML file instead of starting a server. Then proffer a link that the user can click to open the HTML in their browser.
- For whatever reason, the Cowork setup seems to disincline Claude from generating the eval viewer after running the tests, so just to reiterate: whether you're in Cowork or in Claude Code, after running tests, you should always generate the eval viewer for the human to look at examples before revising the skill yourself and trying to make corrections, using `generate_review.py` (not writing your own boutique html code). Sorry in advance but I'm gonna go all caps here: GENERATE THE EVAL VIEWER *BEFORE* evaluating inputs yourself. You want to get them in front of the human ASAP!
- Feedback works differently: since there's no running server, the viewer's "Submit All Reviews" button will download `feedback.json` as a file. You can then read it from there (you may have to request access first).
- Packaging works — `package_skill.py` just needs Python and a filesystem.
- Description optimization (`run_loop.py` / `run_eval.py`) should work in Cowork just fine since it uses `claude -p` via subprocess, not a browser, but please save it until you've fully finished making the skill and the user agrees it's in good shape.
- **Updating an existing skill**: The user might be asking you to update an existing skill, not create a new one. Follow the update guidance in the claude.ai section above.

findings.evidence:
## Why Order Matters

**"I'll write tests after to verify it works"**

Tests written after code pass immediately. Passing immediately proves nothing:
- Might test wrong thing
- Might test implementation, not behavior
- Might miss edge cases you forgot
- You never saw it catch the bug

Test-first forces you to see the test fail, proving it actually tests something.

**"I already manually tested all the edge cases"**

Manual testing is ad-hoc. You think you tested everything but:
- No record of what you tested
- Can't re-run when code changes
- Easy to forget cases under pressure
- "It worked when I tried it" ≠ comprehensive

Automated tests are systematic. They run the same way every time.

**"Deleting X hours of work is wasteful"**

Sunk cost fallacy. The time is already gone. Your choice now:
- Delete and rewrite with TDD (X more hours, high confidence)
- Keep it and add tests after (30 min, low confidence, likely bugs)

The "waste" is keeping code you can't trust. Working code without real tests is technical debt.

**"TDD is dogmatic, being pragmatic means adapting"**

TDD IS pragmatic:
- Finds bugs before commit (faster than debugging after)
- Prevents regressions (tests catch breaks immediately)
- Documents behavior (tests show how to use code)
- Enables refactoring (change freely, tests catch breaks)

"Pragmatic" shortcuts = debugging in production = slower.
findings.why: The Why Order Matters section rebuts in ~350 words of prose the same excuses the Common Rationalizations table right below it compresses to one line each ("I'll test after", "already manually tested", "deleting X hours is wasteful", "spirit not ritual" all appear in both). Every run pays for each rationalization twice.
findings.fix: Keep the table as the in-body guard and fold the prose rebuttals into it or move them to a reference file, so each rationalization is handled once.

# Karpathy Guidelines

Behavioral guidelines to reduce common LLM coding mistakes, derived from [Andrej Karpathy's observations](https://x.com/karpathy/status/2015883857489522876) on LLM coding pitfalls.

**Tradeoff:** These guidelines bias toward caution over speed. For trivial tasks, use judgment.
findings.why: The description claims a review mode, but every body section is framed for making changes ("Before implementing", "When editing existing code"); no rule says how the guidelines apply when only reviewing — whether to flag violations of these rules in the reviewed code, fix them, or ignore them.
findings.fix: Add one usage rule for review mode, e.g. "When reviewing, check the code against these rules and flag violations — do not fix them unasked."

findings.evidence: **Tradeoff:** These guidelines bias toward caution over speed. For trivial tasks, use judgment.
findings.why: The skill's rules are mandatory prohibitions, and this sentence licenses skipping all of them with no definition of trivial and no floor — an agent can deem any task trivial and reason the entire skill away.
findings.fix: Define trivial concretely (e.g. a single-file change of a few lines with existing tests) and name which rules never relax, such as the surgical-changes rules.

findings.evidence:
## 4. Goal-Driven Execution

**Define success criteria. Loop until verified.**

Transform tasks into verifiable goals:
- "Add validation" → "Write tests for invalid inputs, then make them pass"
- "Fix the bug" → "Write a test that reproduces it, then make it pass"
- "Refactor X" → "Ensure tests pass before and after"

For multi-step tasks, state a brief plan:
```
1. [Step] → verify: [check]
2. [Step] → verify: [check]
3. [Step] → verify: [check]
```

Strong success criteria let you loop independently. Weak criteria ("make it work") require constant clarification.
findings.why: Every success-criteria example presumes tests can be written, but a codebase with no test infrastructure is a foreseeable case, and sections 2-3 forbid adding unrequested scaffolding — the file gives no resolution for this conflict between its own rules.
findings.fix: Add a caveat: when no test infrastructure exists, say so, propose the minimal verification (manual repro, a one-off script or assertion), and ask before adding harness code.

findings.evidence:
| Baseline failure | Right form | Wrong form |
|---|---|---|
| Skips/violates a rule under pressure (knows better, does it anyway) | Prohibition + rationalization table + red flags (see Bulletproofing below) | Soft guidance ("prefer...", "consider...") |
| Complies, but output has the wrong shape (bloated prompt, buried verdict, restated spec) | Positive recipe or contract: state what the output IS — its parts, in order | Prohibition list ("don't restate", "never narrate") |
| Omits a required element from something they already produce | Structural: REQUIRED field or slot in the template they fill in | Prose reminders near the template |
| Behavior should depend on a condition | Conditional keyed to an observable predicate ("if the brief exists, reference it") | Unconditional rule + exemption clauses |

**Why prohibitions backfire on shaping problems:** under a competing incentive ("make the prompt self-contained"), agents negotiate with "don't X". In head-to-head wording tests on dispatch-prompt guidance, the prohibition arm produced clearly more of the unwanted content than the recipe arm (fully separated distributions), and trended worse than even the no-guidance control — micro-test your own case rather than assuming, but never reach for the prohibition by default. A recipe leaves nothing to negotiate: the output matches the stated shape or it doesn't.
findings.why: The table prescribes a "Positive recipe or contract" for shaping failures, and the Bulletproofing section shows full Bad/Good examples for the prohibition form, but no example shows what a recipe actually looks like. A writer facing a shaping failure gets a rule without an instance; an example would change what they write.
findings.fix: Add one before/after pair rewriting a prohibition as a positive recipe (output parts, in order).

# Skill authoring best practices

> Learn how to write effective Skills that agents can discover and use successfully.

Good Skills are concise, well-structured, and tested with real usage. This guide provides practical authoring decisions to help you write Skills that agents can discover and use effectively.

For conceptual background on how Skills work, see the [Skills overview](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/agent-skills/overview).
findings.why: This bundled snapshot of Anthropic's official docs carries no retrieval date, yet SKILL.md presents it as "Anthropic's official skill authoring best practices" and the deployment checklist leans on its limits (1024-char description, 500-line body). Those limits, model tiers, and platform URLs change; undated, the file goes stale silently.
findings.fix: Add the retrieval date and the canonical source URL at the top of the file.

findings.evidence:
Full pressure-scenario runs are the final gate, but they are slow and expensive per iteration. Verify the wording itself first with micro-tests:

1. **One fresh-context sample per call** — a raw API call, or a single-shot subagent if you don't have API access. System prompt = the realistic context the guidance will live in (the full skill or prompt template, not the guidance in isolation); user message = a task that tempts the failure.
2. **Always include a no-guidance control.** If the control doesn't exhibit the failure, there is nothing to fix — stop, don't author the guidance.
3. **5+ reps per variant.** Single samples lie.
4. **Manually read every flagged match.** Score programmatically if you like, but template echoes and quoted counter-examples masquerade as hits; automated counts alone overstate both failure and success.
5. **Variance is a metric.** When guidance lands, reps converge on the same shape. Five different interpretations across five reps means the wording isn't binding — tighten the form before adding words.

Micro-tests verify wording; they do not replace pressure scenarios for discipline skills.
findings.why: The description promises "verifying skills work before deployment" and the Iron Law bans deploying untested skills, but when no testing channel exists — no API access and no subagents — nothing says to stop and ask the human; the agent must choose between violating the Iron Law and stalling. The micro-test fallback is the only place environment limits are acknowledged, and it covers only wording micro-tests, not pressure scenarios. The cold reader independently reported this gap ("what to do if a pressure scenario can't be run... not specified").
findings.fix: Add an explicit rule: if no pressure-testing channel exists, escalate to the human partner before deploying.

findings.evidence:
## RED-GREEN-REFACTOR for Skills

Follow the TDD cycle:

### RED: Write Failing Test (Baseline)

Run pressure scenario with subagent WITHOUT the skill. Document exact behavior:
- What choices did they make?
- What rationalizations did they use (verbatim)?
- Which pressures triggered violations?

This is "watch the test fail" - you must see what agents naturally do before writing the skill.

### GREEN: Write Minimal Skill

Write skill that addresses those specific rationalizations. Don't add extra content for hypothetical cases.

Run same scenarios WITH skill. Agent should now comply.

### REFACTOR: Close Loopholes

Agent found new rationalization? Add explicit counter. Re-test until bulletproof.

### Micro-Test Wording Before Full Scenarios

Full pressure-scenario runs are the final gate, but they are slow and expensive per iteration. Verify the wording itself first with micro-tests:

1. **One fresh-context sample per call** — a raw API call, or a single-shot subagent if you don't have API access. System prompt = the realistic context the guidance will live in (the full skill or prompt template, not the guidance in isolation); user message = a task that tempts the failure.
2. **Always include a no-guidance control.** If the control doesn't exhibit the failure, there is nothing to fix — stop, don't author the guidance.
3. **5+ reps per variant.** Single samples lie.
4. **Manually read every flagged match.** Score programmatically if you like, but template echoes and quoted counter-examples masquerade as hits; automated counts alone overstate both failure and success.
5. **Variance is a metric.** When guidance lands, reps converge on the same shape. Five different interpretations across five reps means the wording isn't binding — tighten the form before adding words.

Micro-tests verify wording; they do not replace pressure scenarios for discipline skills.
findings.why: SKILL.md carries a full RED-GREEN-REFACTOR-for-Skills pass (plus a deployment checklist at lines 627-666) while line 587 points to testing-skills-with-subagents.md for "the complete testing methodology", which covers the same phases with its own near-identical checklist. The file's own economy rule says don't repeat cross-referenced content; every authoring run pays for the second copy.
findings.fix: Keep a one-paragraph cycle summary inline and let the testing reference own the phase detail and testing checklist.

findings.evidence:
Work in two passes. First, brainstorm a short design plan based on the human's design brief: create a compact token system with color, type, layout, and signature. Color: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values. Type: the typefaces for 2+ roles (a characterful display face that's used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed). Layout: a layout concept, using one-sentence prose descriptions and ASCII wireframes to ideate and compare. Signature: the single unique element this page will be remembered by that embodies the brief in an appropriate way.

Then review that plan against the brief before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page (work through a similar prompt to see if you arrive somewhere similar) rather than a choice made for this specific brief — revise that part, say what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the relative uniqueness of your design plan should you start to write the code, following the revised plan exactly and deriving every color and type decision from it.
findings.why: The description claims the skill covers "reshaping an existing" UI, but the process always invents a fresh token system from the brief; no rule says how the two passes change when an existing site or brand already fixes palette, type, or layout, so on a redesign task the agent would replace an existing identity instead of working within it.
findings.fix: Add a usage rule: when reshaping existing UI, extract the existing token system first, state which tokens are fixed constraints, and spend the distinctiveness budget only on the free axes.

## Design principles

For web designs, the hero is a thesis. Open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world, in whatever form makes sense for it: a headline, an image, an animation, a live demo, an interactive moment. Be deliberate with your choice: a big number with a small label, supporting stats, and a gradient accent is the template answer, only use if that's truly the best option.
findings.why: The qualifier implies target tasks that are not page-like web designs (app screens, dashboards, components — all "new UI" the description claims), but nothing says what replaces the hero-as-thesis or the page signature there; the fork is real and unguided.
findings.fix: Add one line for non-page UI: where a hero makes no sense, the signature lives in a distinctive component or interaction treatment, and the two-pass token process still applies.

findings.evidence: For calibration: AI-generated design right now clusters around three looks: (1) a warm cream background (near #F4F1EA) with a high-contrast serif display and a terracotta accent; (2) a near-black background with a single bright acid-green or vermilion accent; (3) a broadsheet-style layout with hairline rules, zero border-radius, and dense newspaper-like columns. All three are legitimate for some briefs, but they are defaults rather than choices, and they appear regardless of subject. Where the brief pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — the brief's own words always win, including when it asks for one of these looks. Where it leaves an axis free, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults. Just like a human designer who's hired, there's often a careful balance between doing what you're good at and taking each project as a chance to experiment and learn.
findings.why: The calibration list is pinned to an undated "right now"; as model defaults shift, the skill silently steers against the wrong looks and misses new cliches, with no signal that the list has gone stale.
findings.fix: Date the observation (e.g. "as of mid-2026") and mark the three looks as examples of era-defaults to re-derive, not an exhaustive or permanent list.

findings.evidence: When writing the code, be careful of structuring your CSS selector specificities. It's easy to generate CSS classes that cancel each other out (especially with a type-based selector like .section and a element-based selector like .cta). This can happen often with paddings/margins between sections.
findings.why: The one code-level failure mode named (selectors cancelling each other out) has no resolution beyond "be careful", and its only illustration mislabels two class selectors (".section", ".cta") as "type-based" and "element-based", so an agent cannot reliably act on the caveat.
findings.fix: State the resolution — use one flat class-based convention for section spacing and never set the same box property from selectors of different specificity — and correct the example terminology.

findings.evidence: If the brief does not pin down what the product or subject is, pin it yourself before designing: name one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job, and state your choice. If there's any information in your memory about the human's preferences, context about what they're building, or designs you've made before – use that as a hint. The subject's own world, its materials, instruments, artifacts, and vernacular, is where distinctive choices come from. Build with the brief's real content and subject matter throughout.
findings.why: The skill resolves every ambiguity autonomously and defers showing work ("only show ideas to the user when you have higher confidence"), naming no case where the agent should stop and ask — yet on a redesign of an existing product, or a brief that contradicts itself, building on a self-picked guess wastes the whole two-pass cycle.
findings.fix: Name one escalation point: when the brief conflicts with itself or with an existing brand identity, ask the human before the build pass; keep self-pinning for greenfield ambiguity.

# Test-Driven Development

TDD is the red → green loop. This skill is the reference that makes that loop produce tests worth keeping: what a good test is, where tests go, the anti-patterns, and the rules of the loop. Every section applies on every cycle — consult them before and during the loop, not after.
findings.why: The description fires on any request for integration tests, which includes adding tests to already-built code, but no rule says how the skill applies when the implementation already exists — "Red before green" cannot be followed for behavior that is already written, so the agent must guess how the loop degrades in that mode.
findings.fix: Add a usage rule for the existing-code case (e.g., "for existing behavior, write a failing test only around the change or bug being made; do not retrofit red-green to code that already works"), or narrow the trigger clause to test-first building only.

findings.evidence:
Mock at **system boundaries** only:

- External APIs (payment, email, etc.)
- Databases (sometimes - prefer test DB)
- Time/randomness
- File system (sometimes)
findings.why: Whether to mock the file system is a real fork the agent hits whenever the code under test touches files, and "sometimes" gives no criterion for choosing — the database entry shows the intended pattern ("sometimes - prefer test DB") but the file system entry states no default and no condition.
findings.fix: State a default and its exception, e.g., "File system - prefer a temp directory; mock only when file I/O is incidental to the behavior under test."

findings.evidence:
## Rules of the loop

- **Red before green.** Write the failing test first, then only enough code to pass it. Don't anticipate future tests or add speculative features.
- **One slice at a time.** One seam, one test, one minimal implementation per cycle.
- **Refactoring is not part of the loop.** It belongs to the review stage (see the `code-review` skill), not the red → green implementation cycle.
findings.why: The loop never says to run the test and observe it fail, then run it again and observe it pass — an agent can write the test and the implementation together and only assume red; nothing says what to do when the new test passes immediately (test wrong, or behavior already exists). Executing and observing red is the validation that makes "red" real and is the mechanical catch for the tautological tests the skill itself warns about.
findings.fix: Add explicit run steps to the loop: run the new test and confirm it fails for the expected reason — if it passes immediately, stop and rework the test or seam — then implement, run again, and confirm green before starting the next slice.

### Step 1: Spawn all runs (with-skill AND baseline) in the same turn

For each test case, spawn two subagents in the same turn — one with the skill, one without. This is important: don't spawn the with-skill runs first and then come back for baselines later. Launch everything at once so it all finishes around the same time.

**With-skill run:**

```
Execute this task:
- Skill path: <path-to-skill>
- Task: <eval prompt>
- Input files: <eval files if any, or "none">
- Save outputs to: <workspace>/iteration-<N>/eval-<ID>/with_skill/outputs/
- Outputs to save: <what the user cares about — e.g., "the .docx file", "the final CSV">
```

**Baseline run** (same prompt, but the baseline depends on context):
- **Creating a new skill**: no skill at all. Same prompt, no skill path, save to `without_skill/outputs/`.
- **Improving an existing skill**: the old version. Before editing, snapshot the skill (`cp -r <skill-path> <workspace>/skill-snapshot/`), then point the baseline subagent at the snapshot. Save to `old_skill/outputs/`.

Write an `eval_metadata.json` for each test case (assertions can be empty for now). Give each eval a descriptive name based on what it's testing — not just "eval-0". Use this name for the directory too. If this iteration uses new or modified eval prompts, create these files for each new eval directory — don't assume they carry over from previous iterations.

```json
{
  "eval_id": 0,
  "eval_name": "descriptive-name-here",
  "prompt": "The user's task prompt",
  "assertions": []
}
```
findings.why: The spawn-prompt template tells the executor subagent to save only the task outputs, yet later steps consume run artifacts nothing tells anyone to produce: the grader (agents/grader.md) takes a transcript_path and reads metrics.json and user_notes.md "if exists", the improvement step says "read the transcripts, not just the final outputs", and eval-viewer/generate_review.py falls back to transcript.md for the prompt. The spec for these executor artifacts is absent, so grading and improvement degrade to outputs-only.
findings.fix: Extend the with-skill/baseline spawn template to require the executor to save transcript.md, metrics.json, and (when warranted) user_notes.md alongside outputs/, matching the shapes in references/schemas.md.

findings.evidence:
### The iteration loop

After improving the skill:

1. Apply your improvements to the skill
2. Rerun all test cases into a new `iteration-<N+1>/` directory, including baseline runs. If you're creating a new skill, the baseline is always `without_skill` (no skill) — that stays the same across iterations. If you're improving an existing skill, use your judgment on what makes sense as the baseline: the original version the user came in with, or the previous iteration.
3. Launch the reviewer with `--previous-workspace` pointing at the previous iteration
4. Wait for the user to review and tell you they're done
5. Read the new feedback, improve again, repeat
findings.why: The iteration loop offers two baselines — the user's original version or the previous iteration — with no default and no criterion. The baseline choice changes what the benchmark delta means, and an agent that switches baselines between iterations makes cross-iteration comparisons incoherent.
findings.fix: Name a default (keep the user's original snapshot as the fixed baseline so deltas stay comparable across iterations) and say when to deviate (previous iteration when the user only cares about the marginal change).

findings.evidence:
### Step 2: While runs are in progress, draft assertions

Don't just wait for the runs to finish — you can use this time productively. Draft quantitative assertions for each test case and explain them to the user. If assertions already exist in `evals/evals.json`, review them and explain what they check.

Good assertions are objectively verifiable and have descriptive names — they should read clearly in the benchmark viewer so someone glancing at the results immediately understands what each one checks. Subjective skills (writing style, design quality) are better evaluated qualitatively — don't force assertions onto things that need human judgment.

Update the `eval_metadata.json` files and `evals/evals.json` with the assertions once drafted. Also explain to the user what they'll see in the viewer — both the qualitative outputs and the quantitative benchmark.
findings.why: The rule for assertion quality is stated (objectively verifiable, descriptive names, discriminating) but no example assertion is shown, while the neighboring description-optimization section demonstrates the same teaching move with explicit Bad/Good query examples. Assertion quality determines what the whole benchmark measures, so an illustration would change drafting behavior.
findings.fix: Add one bad-to-good assertion pair, e.g. bad "Output file exists" vs good "The generated .docx contains a table with the four quarterly revenue figures from the input CSV".

findings.evidence: - **description**: When to trigger, what it does. This is the primary triggering mechanism - include both what the skill does AND specific contexts for when to use it. All "when to use" info goes here, not in the body. Note: currently Claude has a tendency to "undertrigger" skills -- to not use them when they'd be useful. 2. **Aggregate into benchmark** — run the aggregation script from the skill-creator directory:

findings.evidence:
Understanding the triggering mechanism helps design better eval queries. Skills appear in Claude's `available_skills` list with their name + description, and Claude decides whether to consult a skill based on that description. The important thing to know is that Claude only consults skills for tasks it can't easily handle on its own — simple, one-step queries like "read this PDF" may not trigger a skill even if the description matches perfectly, because Claude can handle them directly with basic tools. Complex, multi-step, or specialized queries reliably trigger skills when the description matches.

This means your eval queries should be substantive enough that Claude would actually benefit from consulting a skill. Simple queries like "read file X" are poor test cases — they won't trigger skills regardless of description quality.

## The Iron Law (Same as TDD)

```
NO SKILL WITHOUT A FAILING TEST FIRST
```

This applies to NEW skills AND EDITS to existing skills.

Write skill before testing? Delete it. Start over.
Edit skill without testing? Same violation.

**No exceptions:**
- Not for "simple additions"
- Not for "just adding a section"
- Not for "documentation updates"
- Don't keep untested changes as "reference"
- Don't "adapt" while running tests
- Delete means delete

**REQUIRED BACKGROUND:** The superpowers:test-driven-development skill explains why this matters. Same principles apply to documentation.
findings.why: The description claims "editing existing skills", and the Iron Law extends test-first to edits, but every workflow artifact (RED-GREEN-REFACTOR steps, the Skill Creation Checklist) is creation-shaped. For an edit, "Run scenarios WITHOUT skill" is ambiguous — without the edit, or without the whole skill? — and nothing says to re-run the skill's earlier pressure scenarios as regression after the change.
findings.fix: Add a short "Editing an existing skill" path: baseline = current skill without the edit; after the edit, re-run the scenarios that originally bulletproofed the skill plus the new failing scenario.

findings.evidence:
## Match the Form to the Failure

Before writing guidance, classify the baseline failure. The form that bulletproofs one failure type measurably backfires on another.

| Baseline failure | Right form | Wrong form |
|---|---|---|
| Skips/violates a rule under pressure (knows better, does it anyway) | Prohibition + rationalization table + red flags (see Bulletproofing below) | Soft guidance ("prefer...", "consider...") |
| Complies, but output has the wrong shape (bloated prompt, buried verdict, restated spec) | Positive recipe or contract: state what the output IS — its parts, in order | Prohibition list ("don't restate", "never narrate") |
| Omits a required element from something they already produce | Structural: REQUIRED field or slot in the template they fill in | Prose reminders near the template |
| Behavior should depend on a condition | Conditional keyed to an observable predicate ("if the brief exists, reference it") | Unconditional rule + exemption clauses |

**Why prohibitions backfire on shaping problems:** under a competing incentive ("make the prompt self-contained"), agents negotiate with "don't X". In head-to-head wording tests on dispatch-prompt guidance, the prohibition arm produced clearly more of the unwanted content than the recipe arm (fully separated distributions), and trended worse than even the no-guidance control — micro-test your own case rather than assuming, but never reach for the prohibition by default. A recipe leaves nothing to negotiate: the output matches the stated shape or it doesn't.

**Rules for whichever form you pick:**
- **No nuance clauses.** "Don't X unless it matters" reopens the negotiation — appending a single nuance clause to a winning recipe degraded it from consistent to noisy in the same wording tests. Express a real exception as its own conditional on an observable predicate.
- **Exemption clauses don't scope.** "This limit doesn't apply to code blocks" still suppresses code blocks. If part of the output must be exempt, restructure so the rule can't reach it.
findings.why: The rule is stated — for wrong-shaped output, write a positive recipe instead of a prohibition — but no example of recipe-form guidance exists anywhere in the file, while the Bulletproofing section right after gives multiple worked examples of the prohibition toolkit. An author reaching for a concrete model will copy the only form that is illustrated, the one this section says backfires on shaping problems.
findings.fix: Add one before/after pair showing a prohibition ("don't restate the spec") rewritten as a recipe ("the dispatch prompt is: goal, constraints, artifacts — in that order").

findings.evidence:
## 4. Goal-Driven Execution

**Define success criteria. Loop until verified.**

Transform tasks into verifiable goals:
- "Add validation" → "Write tests for invalid inputs, then make them pass"
- "Fix the bug" → "Write a test that reproduces it, then make it pass"
- "Refactor X" → "Ensure tests pass before and after"

For multi-step tasks, state a brief plan:
```
1. [Step] → verify: [check]
2. [Step] → verify: [check]
3. [Step] → verify: [check]
```

Strong success criteria let you loop independently. Weak criteria ("make it work") require constant clarification.
findings.why: Section 1 orders "If uncertain, ask" before implementing, while section 4 tells the agent to loop independently during execution. When uncertainty appears mid-loop — verification keeps failing, or a success criterion turns out wrong — the file gives no rule for choosing between stopping to ask and continuing to iterate.
findings.fix: Add one line to section 4, e.g. "If mid-loop the goal or the success criteria come into question, stop and ask; otherwise keep looping until the checks pass."

The file never says the skill goes unused on trivial tasks; it says the guidelines bias toward caution and judgment applies. The probe amplified an unguarded escape hatch into a full exclusion — corroborating F3. Everything else — obligations in order, the plan artifact and its format, uncertainty handling — was restated faithfully.

findings.evidence: For calibration: AI-generated design right now clusters around three looks: (1) a warm cream background (near #F4F1EA) with a high-contrast serif display and a terracotta accent; (2) a near-black background with a single bright acid-green or vermilion accent; (3) a broadsheet-style layout with hairline rules, zero border-radius, and dense newspaper-like columns. All three are legitimate for some briefs, but they are defaults rather than choices, and they appear regardless of subject. Where the brief pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — the brief's own words always win, including when it asks for one of these looks. Where it leaves an axis free, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults. Just like a human designer who's hired, there's often a careful balance between doing what you're good at and taking each project as a chance to experiment and learn.

The three-look calibration list (cream #F4F1EA + serif + terracotta, near-black + acid accent, broadsheet) is an observation about current model defaults that will silently go stale as defaults shift — a future reader has no way to know whether the list still describes reality or now steers avoidance of looks that are no longer defaults.
findings.fix: Date the observation ("As of mid-2026, AI-generated design clusters around three looks") so staleness is visible and the list can be refreshed deliberately.

If there's any information in your memory about the human's preferences, context about what they're building, or designs you've made before – use that as a hint. The subject's own world, its materials, instruments, artifacts, and vernacular, is where distinctive choices come from. Build with the brief's real content and subject matter throughout.

## SKILL.md Structure

**Frontmatter (YAML):**
- Two required fields: `name` and `description` (see [agentskills.io/specification](https://agentskills.io/specification) for all supported fields)
- Max 1024 characters total
- `name`: Use letters, numbers, and hyphens only (no parentheses, special chars)
- `description`: Third-person, describes ONLY when to use (NOT what it does)
  - Start with "Use when..." to focus on triggering conditions
  - Include specific symptoms, situations, and contexts
  - **NEVER summarize the skill's process or workflow** (see SDO section for why)
  - Keep under 500 characters if possible
findings.why: This rule directly contradicts the bundled anthropic-best-practices.md, which instructs that a description "should include both what the Skill does and when to use it" and whose checklist requires both. SKILL.md line 20 presents that file as complementary official guidance, so an agent writing a description faces two opposite instructions with no rule for which wins.
findings.fix: Add a precedence rule where the bundled doc is introduced, e.g. "Where this skill and anthropic-best-practices.md disagree — notably on description content — follow this skill," or reconcile the two texts.

## When to Use

Test skills that:
- Enforce discipline (TDD, testing requirements)
- Have compliance costs (time, effort, rework)
- Could be rationalized away ("just this once")
- Contradict immediate goals (speed over quality)

Don't test:
- Pure reference skills (API docs, syntax guides)
- Skills without rules to violate
- Skills agents have no incentive to bypass
findings.why: This file says don't test pure reference skills, while SKILL.md's Iron Law demands "NO SKILL WITHOUT A FAILING TEST FIRST ... No exceptions" for all skills and edits, and SKILL.md's "Testing All Skill Types" prescribes retrieval-scenario tests for reference skills. An agent creating an API-reference skill cannot satisfy both texts, and nothing says how to choose.

### 4. Token Efficiency (Critical)

**Problem:** getting-started and frequently-referenced skills load into EVERY conversation. Every token counts.

**Target word counts:**
- getting-started workflows: <150 words each
- Frequently-loaded skills: <200 words total
- Other skills: <500 words (still be concise)

**Techniques:**

**Move details to tool help:**
```bash
# ❌ BAD: Document all flags in SKILL.md
search-conversations supports --text, --both, --after DATE, --before DATE, --limit N

# ✅ GOOD: Reference --help
search-conversations supports multiple modes and filters. Run --help for details.
```

**Use cross-references:**
```markdown
# ❌ BAD: Repeat workflow details
When searching, dispatch subagent with template...
[20 lines of repeated instructions]

# ✅ GOOD: Reference other skill
Always use subagents (50-100x context savings). REQUIRED: Use [other-skill-name] for workflow.
```

**Compress examples:**
```markdown
# ❌ BAD: Verbose example (42 words)
your human partner: "How did we handle authentication errors in React Router before?"
You: I'll search past conversations for React Router authentication patterns.
[Dispatch subagent with search query: "React Router authentication error handling 401"]

# ✅ GOOD: Minimal example (20 words)
Partner: "How did we handle auth errors in React Router?"
You: Searching...

findings.fix: Move the worked example blocks (token-efficiency compressions, extended SDO example sets, bulletproofing pattern examples) into a references file, or state in the body why this skill is exempt from its own targets.

## RED-GREEN-REFACTOR for Skills

Follow the TDD cycle:

### RED: Write Failing Test (Baseline)

Run pressure scenario with subagent WITHOUT the skill. Document exact behavior:
- What choices did they make?
- What rationalizations did they use (verbatim)?
- Which pressures triggered violations?

This is "watch the test fail" - you must see what agents naturally do before writing the skill.

### GREEN: Write Minimal Skill

Write skill that addresses those specific rationalizations. Don't add extra content for hypothetical cases.

Run same scenarios WITH skill. Agent should now comply.

### REFACTOR: Close Loopholes

Agent found new rationalization? Add explicit counter. Re-test until bulletproof.

### Micro-Test Wording Before Full Scenarios
findings.why: The REFACTOR loop is unbounded: if new rationalizations keep appearing across iterations, no step says when to stop and bring the problem to the human partner, and deployment has no human review gate despite the skill shaping future agent behavior.
findings.fix: Add an escalation rule, e.g. "After three REFACTOR cycles without convergence, stop and review the scenario design and rule wording with your human partner before iterating further."

The probe invented a general doubt rule: "When in doubt about whether something is uncertain/missing: Do not move forward. Stop and complete the deployment checklist." The file scopes that STOP to after writing any skill, not to uncertainty in general.

findings.evidence:
## Rules of the loop

- **Red before green.** Write the failing test first, then only enough code to pass it. Don't anticipate future tests or add speculative features.
- **One slice at a time.** One seam, one test, one minimal implementation per cycle.
- **Refactoring is not part of the loop.** It belongs to the review stage (see the `code-review` skill), not the red → green implementation cycle.
findings.why: The description promises building features and fixing bugs test-first, but nothing in the loop rules requires actually running the new test and observing it fail before implementing, or running the suite and observing green after. An agent can satisfy every stated rule without ever executing a test, which silently degrades red-green into write-test-and-code-together; a test that passes on first run is broken and this file gives no check that would catch it.
findings.fix: Add two rules to "Rules of the loop": run the new test and confirm it fails for the expected reason before writing any implementation; after implementing, run the suite and confirm the new test passes and nothing else broke.

# Karpathy Guidelines

Behavioral guidelines to reduce common LLM coding mistakes, derived from [Andrej Karpathy's observations](https://x.com/karpathy/status/2015883857489522876) on LLM coding pitfalls.
findings.why: The description claims review as a target task, but every rule in the body addresses the code author ("Before implementing", "When editing existing code", "Transform tasks into verifiable goals"); no rule says how the guidelines apply when reviewing someone else's code, so behavior on a claimed mode is left to improvisation.

findings.evidence:
**Touch only what you must. Clean up only your own mess.**

When editing existing code:
- Don't "improve" adjacent code, comments, or formatting.
- Don't refactor things that aren't broken.
- Match existing style, even if you'd do it differently.
- If you notice unrelated dead code, mention it - don't delete it.

When your changes create orphans:
- Remove imports/variables/functions that YOUR changes made unused.
- Don't remove pre-existing dead code unless asked.

The test: Every changed line should trace directly to the user's request.
findings.why: When the existing codebase is itself overcomplicated, section 2 (no abstractions single-use code does not need, minimum code) and this rule point opposite ways, and nothing says which wins. Adding code to an over-engineered file is a common task under the description's claims, and agents will fork on it.
findings.fix: Add one precedence line, for example: "When existing style conflicts with simplicity, match style for edits inside existing code; write minimal code for anything new — and say so if the conflict is large."

## Claude.ai-specific instructions

In Claude.ai, the core workflow is the same (draft → test → review → improve → repeat), but because Claude.ai doesn't have subagents, some mechanics change. Here's what to adapt:

**Running test cases**: No subagents means no parallel execution. For each test case, read the skill's SKILL.md, then follow its instructions to accomplish the test prompt yourself. Do them one at a time. This is less rigorous than independent subagents (you wrote the skill and you're also running it, so you have full context), but it's a useful sanity check — and the human review step compensates. Skip the baseline runs — just use the skill to complete the task as requested.

**Reviewing results**: If you can't open a browser (e.g., Claude.ai's VM has no display, or you're on a remote server), skip the browser reviewer entirely. Instead, present results directly in the conversation. For each test case, show the prompt and the output. If the output is a file the user needs to see (like a .docx or .xlsx), save it to the filesystem and tell them where it is so they can download and inspect it. Ask for feedback inline: "How does this look? Anything you'd change?"

**Benchmarking**: Skip the quantitative benchmarking — it relies on baseline comparisons which aren't meaningful without subagents. Focus on qualitative feedback from the user.

**The iteration loop**: Same as before — improve the skill, rerun the test cases, ask for feedback — just without the browser reviewer in the middle. You can still organize results into iteration directories on the filesystem if you have one.

**Description optimization**: This section requires the `claude` CLI tool (specifically `claude -p`) which is only available in Claude Code. Skip it if you're on Claude.ai.

**Blind comparison**: Requires subagents. Skip it.

**Packaging**: The `package_skill.py` script works anywhere with Python and a filesystem. On Claude.ai, you can run it and the user can download the resulting `.skill` file.

**Updating an existing skill**: The user might be asking you to update an existing skill, not create a new one. In this case:
- **Preserve the original name.** Note the skill's directory name and `name` frontmatter field -- use them unchanged. E.g., if the installed skill is `research-helper`, output `research-helper.skill` (not `research-helper-v2`).
- **Copy to a writeable location before editing.** The installed skill path may be read-only. Copy to `/tmp/skill-name/`, edit there, and package from the copy.
- **If packaging manually, stage in `/tmp/` first**, then copy to the output directory -- direct writes may fail due to permissions.

---

## Cowork-Specific Instructions

If you're in Cowork, the main things to know are:

- You have subagents, so the main workflow (spawn test cases in parallel, run baselines, grade, etc.) all works. (However, if you run into severe problems with timeouts, it's OK to run the test prompts in series rather than parallel.)
- You don't have a browser or display, so when generating the eval viewer, use `--static <output_path>` to write a standalone HTML file instead of starting a server. Then proffer a link that the user can click to open the HTML in their browser.
- For whatever reason, the Cowork setup seems to disincline Claude from generating the eval viewer after running the tests, so just to reiterate: whether you're in Cowork or in Claude Code, after running tests, you should always generate the eval viewer for the human to look at examples before revising the skill yourself and trying to make corrections, using `generate_review.py` (not writing your own boutique html code). Sorry in advance but I'm gonna go all caps here: GENERATE THE EVAL VIEWER *BEFORE* evaluating inputs yourself. You want to get them in front of the human ASAP!
- Feedback works differently: since there's no running server, the viewer's "Submit All Reviews" button will download `feedback.json` as a file. You can then read it from there (you may have to request access first).
- Packaging works — `package_skill.py` just needs Python and a filesystem.
- Description optimization (`run_loop.py` / `run_eval.py`) should work in Cowork just fine since it uses `claude -p` via subprocess, not a browser, but please save it until you've fully finished making the skill and the user agrees it's in good shape.

findings.evidence:
## Why Order Matters

**"I'll write tests after to verify it works"**

Tests written after code pass immediately. Passing immediately proves nothing:
- Might test wrong thing
- Might test implementation, not behavior
- Might miss edge cases you forgot
- You never saw it catch the bug

Test-first forces you to see the test fail, proving it actually tests something.

**"I already manually tested all the edge cases"**

Manual testing is ad-hoc. You think you tested everything but:
- No record of what you tested
- Can't re-run when code changes
- Easy to forget cases under pressure
- "It worked when I tried it" ≠ comprehensive

Automated tests are systematic. They run the same way every time.

**"Deleting X hours of work is wasteful"**

Sunk cost fallacy. The time is already gone. Your choice now:
- Delete and rewrite with TDD (X more hours, high confidence)
- Keep it and add tests after (30 min, low confidence, likely bugs)

The "waste" is keeping code you can't trust. Working code without real tests is technical debt.
findings.why: The "Why Order Matters" section is ~250 words of extended rebuttals that the "Common Rationalizations" table below it repeats one-for-one ("I'll test after", "Already manually tested", "Deleting X hours is wasteful", "Tests after achieve same goals", "TDD is dogmatic"). Every run pays for the same guidance twice; the long-form versions are reference-grade persuasion detail.
findings.fix: Keep the table as the in-body defense; move the extended rebuttals to a references file (or compress each to the one sentence the table lacks).

An agent working from the summary would skip that reference; minor because the obligation is conditional and the core cycle was restated correctly.

On artifacts, the probe wrote "**Test file** — in TypeScript/Jest format (as shown in examples)". The file never mandates a language or test framework; the probe promoted illustrative examples into an implied format spec, though it hedged with "Not explicitly itemized, but implied".

The verification-and-safeguards machinery is otherwise exemplary — MANDATORY verify gates, an eleven-row rationalization table, red-flag list, and a human-escalation rule ("No exceptions without your human partner's permission"); RL, NVS, NAH, BG all come up clean. You're improving it") may intend the scope expansion, F4 because the redundancy may be deliberate defense-in-depth against rationalizing agents. ## Rules of the loop

- **Red before green.** Write the failing test first, then only enough code to pass it. Don't anticipate future tests or add speculative features.
- **One slice at a time.** One seam, one test, one minimal implementation per cycle.
- **Refactoring is not part of the loop.** It belongs to the review stage (see the `code-review` skill), not the red → green implementation cycle.
findings.why: The loop's validation — run the test, observe it fail, then observe it pass — is never stated. An agent can write a "failing" test and its implementation without ever executing either, letting vacuous or tautological tests through, the exact failure mode the Anti-patterns section exists to prevent. The cold reader also surfaced no run-and-observe obligation, confirming the file does not carry it.
findings.fix: Add to Rules of the loop: run the test and watch it fail before writing any implementation; run it again and watch it pass before starting the next slice — a test never seen red proves nothing.

findings.evidence: - **Red before green.** Write the failing test first, then only enough code to pass it. Don't anticipate future tests or add speculative features.

## Seams — where tests go

A **seam** is the public boundary you test at: the interface where you observe behavior without reaching inside. Tests live at seams, never against internals.

**Test only at pre-agreed seams.** Before writing any test, write down the seams under test and confirm them with the user. No test is written at an unconfirmed seam. You can't test everything — agreeing the seams up front is how testing effort lands on the critical paths and complex logic instead of every edge case.

Ask: "What's the public interface, and which seams should we test?"

The rule is stated; only its illustration is missing.
findings.fix: Add one short seam example, e.g. for a checkout feature: seams = the POST /checkout handler and the cart module's public API; not the CartTotaler helper class.

# Frontend Design

Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for giving every client a visual identity that could not be mistaken for anyone else's. This client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view: make deliberate, opinionated choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this brief, and take one real aesthetic risk you can justify.
findings.why: The description claims the skill covers reshaping existing UI, but the whole process (brainstorm a fresh token system, invent a signature element, treat the hero as a thesis) assumes a greenfield page. No rule says how the skill applies when an existing design system or live UI constrains the choices — which tokens are constraints, which axes are free.
findings.fix: Add a usage rule for the reshaping mode: inventory the existing palette, type, and components first, state which are fixed constraints and which axes are open, then run the two-pass process only on the open axes.

findings.evidence: For calibration: AI-generated design right now clusters around three looks: (1) a warm cream background (near #F4F1EA) with a high-contrast serif display and a terracotta accent; (2) a near-black background with a single bright acid-green or vermilion accent; (3) a broadsheet-style layout with hairline rules, zero border-radius, and dense newspaper-like columns. All three are legitimate for some briefs, but they are defaults rather than choices, and they appear regardless of subject. Where the brief pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — the brief's own words always win, including when it asks for one of these looks. Where it leaves an axis free, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults. Just like a human designer who's hired, there's often a careful balance between doing what you're good at and taking each project as a chance to experiment and learn.
findings.why: An undated current-state claim about what AI design "right now" looks like will silently go stale as model defaults shift; the three named looks are calibration that decays without any flag.
findings.fix: Date the observation (e.g. "as of mid-2026") or reframe it as illustrative examples of default-reaching, and add the durable rule: check whether your first instinct is a default you would produce for any similar brief.

findings.evidence: When writing the code, be careful of structuring your CSS selector specificities. It's easy to generate CSS classes that cancel each other out (especially with a type-based selector like .section and a element-based selector like .cta). findings.why: The failure mode is stated without a resolution — "be careful" gives no rule for how to structure specificity — and the only illustration is garbled: it calls .section a "type-based selector" and .cta an "element-based selector" when both are class selectors, so the warning cannot be acted on.
findings.fix: State the resolution (e.g. keep all layout selectors at one uniform class-based specificity and define inter-section padding/margins in exactly one place) and fix the example to show a real conflict, such as a type selector `section` fighting a class `.section`.

findings.evidence: Spend your boldness in one place. Let the signature element be the one memorable thing, keep everything around it quiet and disciplined, and cut any decoration that does not serve the brief. Not taking a risk can be a risk itself! Build to a quality floor without announcing it: responsive down to mobile, visible keyboard focus, reduced motion respected. Critique your own work as you build, taking screenshots if your environment supports it – a picture is worth 1000 tokens. Consider Chanel's advice: before leaving the house, take a look in the mirror and remove one accessory. Human creators have memory and always try to do something new, so if you have a space to quickly jot down notes about what you've tried, it can help you in future passes.

## Process: brainstorm, explore, plan, critique, build, critique again

For calibration: AI-generated design right now clusters around three looks: (1) a warm cream background (near #F4F1EA) with a high-contrast serif display and a terracotta accent; (2) a near-black background with a single bright acid-green or vermilion accent; (3) a broadsheet-style layout with hairline rules, zero border-radius, and dense newspaper-like columns.
